summary:
Analog Hunter — find their twins on Earth before we go to the Moon and Mars

Before astronauts and rovers fly, they rehearse on Earth at analog sites. The challenge notes that places like the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater and Death Valley are used this way — yet their characteristics have never been fully described, and new candidates are waiting to be found.

Analog Hunter turns that open problem into something a classroom can actually do. The student picks one of six real targets (Shackleton rim, a permanently shadowed crater and the Marius Hills pit on the Moon; Jezero, Gale and Arcadia Planitia on Mars), picks a mission goal (rover driving, ice drilling, searching for signs of life, base and power, cave shelter, or balanced exploration), then picks a candidate from 20 Earth sites on a world map and reads a weighted similarity report: what you can test there, what you can’t, and the gaps no place on Earth can close — gravity, vacuum, radiation, day length.

The final step is the challenge’s real question: propose your own candidate. Estimate its features with sliders, tap its location, and an embedded global climate grid checks your estimate against measured temperature, precipitation and latitude — offline.
details:
What it does and how it works

The app is a single HTML file with five tabs:

1. Mission — the challenge brief restated for a school audience: the four selection factors (topography, geology, environment, resources), how to play in five steps, and an honest note that the official challenge page could not be read automatically, so the summary was compiled from pages that reproduce it.

2. Explore — the core loop, in five numbered steps:

  • Pick your target. Six real targets with their own data: coordinates, surface temperature, geology tags, and a “why is it hard?” line (e.g. at Shackleton the Sun never leaves the horizon, so panels must stand upright and shadows run for kilometres; a permanently shadowed crater floor averages −236 °C in Cabeus, where LCROSS found water ice in 2009).
  • Decide what to test. Six goals, each a different weight vector over the six features plus geology. The weight bars are drawn on screen, so the student can see that ice drilling weights subsurface ice ×4 and cold ×3, while the search for life weights geology ×6 and polar light ×0.
  • Pick a candidate. 20 Earth sites on an SVG world map — Atacama, Haughton Crater, Death Valley, McMurdo Dry Valleys, Mauna Loa/Mauna Kea (HI-SEAS), Iceland’s highlands, Lanzarote, Rio Tinto, the Utah MDRS desert, Craters of the Moon, Lake Salda, Lake Tuz, Dallol, Svalbard, the Namib, Pilbara, Ladakh, the Qaidam Basin, Meteor Crater — plus the Amazon Rainforest as a deliberate control site, included so students can see a model fail.
  • Read the similarity report. Score = Σ (1 − |target − site| / 10) × weight / Σ weight, with geology scored as the fraction of the target’s tags the site matches. The report draws target and candidate bars side by side, lists what can and can’t be tested in plain language, and always ends with a “gaps that can’t be closed”table: Earth’s 9.81 m/s² against the Moon’s 1.62; 1013 hPa against about 6 hPa on Mars; 2.4 mSv per year against roughly 0.67 mSv per day on the Martian surface.
  • Propose your own candidate. The student names a place, estimates its features with sliders, picks its geology, then taps its location. Two global 1° climate grids (about 65 KB each, base64-embedded in the file) are read at that point and the cold, aridity and polar-light scores are recomputed from measurement — so the student’s estimate is graded automatically, with no typing and no network.

A mission log awards ★ for 60+ points, ★★ for a top-three finish and ★★★ for finding the best candidate, with ranks from Rookie to Chief Analog Hunter (18 ★ total).

3. Data lab — “how do scientists know this?” Open datasets grouped by world (Moon: Moon Trek, LRO Diviner, Kaguya/DARTS, Chandrayaan/PRADAN, Chang’e, ShadowCam; Mars: Mars Trek, MRO CRISM, SWIM, ESA PSA, USGS Astrogeology; Earth: SRTM, HLS, EMIT, Copernicus), each tagged with the feature it measures. Below it, an accuracy confession: in the first version every value was a guess; three features were later recomputed from measured climate data and latitude, and the report now shows “similarity with first estimate” next to “similarity with real data,” naming the size and direction of the error. Validation across 20 sites: the cold score was off by 0.5 points on average, aridity by 1.6. A six-item matching game (“which data answers which question?”) closes the tab.

4. Classroom — learning outcomes for three bands (grades 1–4, 5–8, 9–12) against the Turkish MEB curriculum with coded outcomes (FB.5.1.2, FB.6.1.1, FB.7.1.1–7.1.3, COĞ.9.1.2, COĞ.9.2.1, COĞ.9.2.3, COĞ.9.3.2) plus NGSS equivalents (4-ESS2-2, MS-ESS1-3, MS-ETS1-2, HS-ETS1-3); a 2 × 40-minute 5E lesson plan with timings; a four-criterion assessment rubric (using data, reasoning, seeing limits, new candidate); and four discussion questions, including “Lake Salda is both a protected natural area and a scientific analog — how can the two be balanced?”

5. Sources — every claim traced, with the grid data, validation method and curriculum pages listed separately. A ten-question quiz with explanations sits above it.

Benefits and intended impact

Most classroom space content asks students to admire. This asks them to decide — and then shows them their decision was a model with a known error bar. The weight vectors make the central insight physical: change the goal and the ranking changes, because “best” is never a property of a place alone. The control site and the gaps table do the opposite work: they teach that an analog is a partial match, and that no site on Earth will ever give you one-sixth gravity.

Step 5 is the part that reaches past the classroom. The challenge asks for new analog sites, and a student in Konya or Burdur can propose one, have a global climate grid test their estimate on the spot, and then plan which satellite dataset would verify the rest. The package already ships two under-studied candidates as examples — Lake Tuz, flagged explicitly as “not an established analog, but worth investigating,” and three Turkish presets: Meke Maar and Karapınar, the Kula volcanic field, and the Nemrut Caldera.

Tools used

  • Languages: HTML5, CSS3 (custom properties, automatic light/dark theme), vanilla JavaScript (ES6+). No library, framework, CDN script or build step; zero network requests at runtime. One .html file, ~219 KB. The only external reference is a Google Fonts stylesheet for Atkinson Hyperlegible Next and Unbounded, which falls back to system fonts if unavailable.
  • Graphics: hand-written SVG throughout — planet discs with radial gradients, the world map and its pins, score rings, comparison bars. No canvas, no images, no bitmaps.
  • Data: every target, site, dataset entry, quiz item and curriculum outcome is an inline JavaScript structure. Two global 1° grids (ERA-Interim 2 m temperature; GPCP v2.2 monthly precipitation, 1979–2010 mean) are compressed to Uint8Arrays and base64-embedded, decoded with atob at load, so custom-candidate verification works with no server.
  • Persistence: localStorage (analog-hunter-v1) for target, goal, sites tried, best stars, quiz and matching state.
  • Accessibility: Atkinson Hyperlegible as the body face, aria-pressed / aria-label on every control, keyboard-focusable map pins, prefers-reduced-motion respected on scroll, and a light/dark theme that follows prefers-color-scheme.

Creativity and what the team considered

  • The model is the subject, not the backdrop. The score formula is printed, the weights are drawn, and the app says outright: “This is a teaching model… The comparison is in the Data section.” A student who wants to argue with the score has everything needed to do it — which is exactly the rubric’s “Advanced” band.
  • We shipped our own error. Rather than quietly fixing the first version’s guessed values, we kept both numbers side by side and label which estimates were off by more than two points in red. Showing a model being corrected by data is the lesson.
  • A control site on purpose. The Amazon is in the list to score near zero. A model that cannot fail teaches nothing.
  • We named what we could not verify. The official challenge page is not machine-readable, so the brief is sourced from pages that reproduce it, and the resource list is flagged as “not the official list — check the challenge page.” Ruggedness, subsurface ice, bare surface and geology tags are still labelled approximate estimates, while cold, aridity and polar light are marked as computed from measurement. Station temperatures are stated as the nearest station, not the site itself, with each station linked.
  • Ethics inside the science. Lake Salda is a protected area and an analog at once; the discussion questions and the high-school activities put scientific fieldwork in protected places on the table rather than treating site selection as a purely technical problem.
  • Localization both ways. Turkish MEB coded outcomes and three Turkish field presets sit alongside NGSS equivalents, so the package is usable in our own classroom and legible to an international judge.
  • Copyright hygiene. Every visual is original SVG we wrote; no NASA or third-party imagery is embedded, only credited by link. The embedded climate grids are openly published scientific datasets, cited with their source and provider.
